subject: General Knowledge
topic: Famous battles of India — mixed tiers

questions.stem: The First Battle of Tarain (1191) is celebrated as a notable Rajput resistance against the Ghurid invasion. Which ruler defeated Muhammad of Ghor's forces in this battle?

options.option_text: Rana Sanga of Mewar, the Rajput confederation chief
Prithviraj Chauhan, ruler of the Chahamana dynasty
Jayachandra of the Gahadavala dynasty of Varanasi
Paramardideva of the Chandela dynasty of Bundelkhand

questions.explanation: Prithviraj Chauhan III of the Chahamana dynasty won the First Battle of Tarain (1191) and captured Muhammad of Ghor, but magnanimously released him — a decision that proved fatal, as Ghor returned in 1192 and defeated Prithviraj at the Second Battle of Tarain. Rana Sanga belonged to the 16th century, well after this event. Jayachandra of Gahadavala was actually a rival of Prithviraj and reportedly aided the Ghurids at the Second Battle of Tarain.

questions.stem: At the Battle of Haldighati (1576), Emperor Akbar sent a Mughal army against Maharana Pratap of Mewar. Who commanded those Mughal forces on the battlefield?

options.option_text: Birbal, Akbar's legendary court poet and close adviser
Man Singh I, the Raja of Amber in Akbar's service
Todar Mal, Akbar's celebrated revenue reform minister
Abdur Rahim Khan-i-Khana, Akbar's trusted senior general

questions.explanation: Man Singh I of Amber (Jaipur), a Rajput chieftain loyal to Akbar, commanded the Mughal army at Haldighati. This choice was deliberate — Akbar sent a fellow Rajput to emphasise Maharana Pratap's isolation. Birbal died in the Yusufzai campaign (1586) and was never a battlefield commander. Todar Mal was primarily an administrator known for the Todar Mal Bandobast (revenue settlement). Abdur Rahim commanded in the Deccan campaigns, not at Haldighati.

questions.stem: The Battle of Samugarh (1658), fought near Agra, was the decisive engagement in the Mughal war of succession. Whose defeat in this battle effectively ended his claim to the Mughal throne?

options.option_text: Shah Shuja, the Governor of Bengal and Bihar
Dara Shikoh, Shah Jahan's designated favourite successor
Murad Bakhsh, the Governor of Gujarat and Malwa
Suleiman Shikoh, Dara's eldest son and Mughal prince

questions.explanation: Aurangzeb, allied with Murad Bakhsh, defeated Dara Shikoh at Samugarh, ending the latter's bid for the throne. Dara Shikoh was Shah Jahan's chosen heir and the most liberal of his sons. The tempting distractor is Murad Bakhsh — he fought alongside Aurangzeb at Samugarh, not against him. Aurangzeb later imprisoned Murad and had him executed in 1661. Shah Shuja was defeated separately at Khajwa (1659).

questions.stem: The Battle of Assaye (1803), fought during the Second Anglo-Maratha War, was a hard-won British victory over the Maratha Confederacy. The British commander who won here later led the allied forces that defeated Napoleon at Waterloo (1815). Who was he?

options.option_text: Robert Clive, later 1st Baron Clive of Plassey
Arthur Wellesley, later the 1st Duke of Wellington
Charles Cornwallis, later 2nd Earl and 1st Marquess
Gerard Lake, later 1st Viscount Lake of Delhi city

questions.explanation: Arthur Wellesley commanded the British forces at Assaye and later called it the finest action he ever fought. He subsequently became the Duke of Wellington and defeated Napoleon at Waterloo in 1815. Robert Clive was associated with Plassey (1757) — a century earlier. Cornwallis is remembered for the Third Mysore War and the Permanent Settlement, not Assaye. Gerard Lake won at Delhi and Laswari (1803) but not at Assaye.

questions.stem: The Battle of Karnal (1739) exposed the hollowness of late Mughal military power. Which Mughal emperor was routed by Nadir Shah's forces in this battle?

options.option_text: Farrukhsiyar, who was deposed by the Sayyid Brothers
Muhammad Shah (Rangeela), reigning Mughal emperor in 1739
Ahmad Shah Bahadur, who succeeded Muhammad Shah in 1748
Alamgir II, who ruled the Mughal empire from 1754–1759

questions.explanation: Muhammad Shah, nicknamed 'Rangeela' for his love of art and pleasure, was the reigning Mughal emperor in 1739 and was humiliatingly defeated at Karnal. Nadir Shah then sacked Delhi and extracted a massive tribute. Farrukhsiyar had already been assassinated in 1719 by the Sayyid Brothers — 20 years before Karnal. Ahmad Shah Bahadur and Alamgir II both ruled after Muhammad Shah and are common temporal distractors.

questions.stem: After his victory at Karnal (1739), Nadir Shah looted the Mughal treasury in Delhi, carrying away two priceless symbols of Mughal imperial wealth. Which pair CORRECTLY identifies what he took back to Persia?

options.option_text: The Kohinoor diamond and the Taj-ul-Kalam (royal seal)
The Kohinoor diamond and the Peacock Throne (Takht-e-Taus)
The Peacock Throne and the Babur-nama illuminated manuscript
The Kohinoor diamond and the Akbar-nama historical chronicle

questions.explanation: Nadir Shah carried both the Kohinoor diamond (then set in the Mughal emperor's turban) and the famed Peacock Throne (Takht-e-Taus), crafted under Shah Jahan — together worth an estimated 700 million rupees. The tempting trap is Option C, because Nadir Shah did also acquire the Daria-i-Noor, but the Babur-nama was not taken; it remained in Mughal custody. Options A and D (Taj-ul-Kalam, Akbar-nama) are plausible-sounding but incorrect pairings invented to test precision of recall.

questions.stem: Humayun's crushing defeat at the Battle of Chausa (1539) at the hands of Sher Shah Suri forced him into a dramatic escape. According to historical accounts, which water body did he cross — reportedly clinging to an inflated skin bag held by a water-carrier named Nizam?

options.option_text: The Yamuna river near Agra, where he re-gathered his forces
The Ganga river near Chausa, crossing on an inflated skin bag
The Ghaghra (Saryu) river, site of his earlier Afghan victory
The Indus river at Attock, the boundary of his eventual exile

questions.explanation: Chausa lies on the south bank of the Ganga near Buxar. After the defeat, Humayun barely escaped by crossing the Ganga on a mashak (inflated animal skin) held by a water-carrier named Nizam, whom Humayun later rewarded by granting him one day's rule over Delhi — a gesture of royal gratitude recorded in Mughal chronicles. The tempting distractor is Option C (Ghaghra), because Humayun did fight the Afghans there in the Battle of Ghaghra (1529), but his 1539 escape was specifically across the Ganga. The Indus (Option D) relates to his later exile to Persia after the Battle of Kanauj (1540).
